title: Reverse the October 2024 capital gains tax rate rise
headline: Back to 10% and 20%, as before October 2024. Costs £2.5bn.
description: Autumn Budget 2024 raised the main rates of capital gains tax to 18% and 24% (from 10% and 20%) and raised the Business Asset Disposal Relief and Investors' Relief rate to 14% and then 18%. Switch this on to reverse the package from April 2027, giving up the Treasury's costing of it (£2.5bn in 2029-30).

baselinePolicy.text: Main rates of capital gains tax 18% and 24% since 30 October 2024, with the Business Asset Disposal Relief and Investors' Relief rate 14% from April 2025 and 18% from April 2026 (Autumn Budget 2024, Table 5.1 line 27).

lines.title: Capital Gains Tax: Increase the main rates of CGT to 18% and 24% from 30 October 2024, and the Business Asset Disposal Relief (BADR) and Investors' Relief (IR) rate to 14% from 6 April 2025 and to 18% from 6 April 2026

rawSource.note: Reversal: the Treasury's costing with its sign reversed for 2027-28 to 2029-30; 2030-31 carries the 2029-30 figure forward with the OBR's capital taxes receipts path.

uprating.head: capitalTaxes
uprating.note: Applied in the years the scorecard covers and extended to 2030-31 with the OBR's capital taxes receipts (ADR-0004).

caveats: The Treasury's line covers the whole package, including the Business Asset Disposal Relief and Investors' Relief changes; the main-rate part cannot be separated from published figures. The costing is on the OBR's October 2024 forecast; the level is not rebased.

considerations.text: The Treasury's scorecard figure is the certified costing of the October 2024 package, including the behavioural response the Treasury and OBR agreed at the time.

The OBR notes that capital gains tax receipts rose about 60% in 2025-26 because disposals were brought forward ahead of the October 2024 rate rise, with the tax paid in January 2026. Timing responses of that kind mean the yield of a rate change in any single year can differ sharply from the steady state.

interactions.text: Both change capital gains tax rates: HMRC's points assume today's 24% rate, while the reversal is costed on the October 2024 forecast, so the combination is approximate.
